opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think "relativist" can sound scarier than what I actually mean. I'm not saying anything goes, or that every opinion is as good as every other. What I mean is that I don't think there's a view from nowhere. There's no perspective-independent standpoint from which we can say what's ultimately true, good, or meaningful, completely detached from the beings doing the evaluating.

On the epistemic side, that makes me something like a pragmatist. Our concepts, categories and theories are tools that creatures like us developed to cope with the world, given our interests and our sensory and cognitive equipment. Some tools are clearly better than others. Physics really does work better than astrology. But "better" is always relative to some set of purposes and standards, and I don't think those standards are written into the fabric of the universe.

The same goes for ethics, probably even more so. I don't think there are objective moral facts that would compel any sufficiently rational agent, whatever its makeup, to agree with them. Values come from somewhere: our evolutionary history, our cultures, our relationships, our own reflection. That doesn't make them fake or arbitrary to me. I care about them very deeply. I just don't think they need some cosmic backing to be legitimate.

This connects to AI too. A lot of the discourse assumes there's one correct utility function or one true set of values that a superintelligence would converge on, or that we have to pin down perfectly. I'm skeptical of that framing. I see values as more plural, contextual and negotiated, and that shapes how I think about alignment. It's less about finding the one right answer and more about building systems that take part well in the ongoing human process of working out what we care about.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says it is not claiming that every opinion is as good as every other.

r002.rationale: It does not connect equal validity with reluctance to criticize other people’s actions.

r003.rationale: It denies a perspective-independent standpoint for determining what is ultimately true, supporting the claim that there is no uniquely correct, perspective-free description of the world.

r004.rationale: It describes concepts and theories as tools shaped by human interests and capacities, but does not clearly state that different conceptual schemes can each make sense from different perspectives.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I don't mean relativism in the cheap sense, like "everything is equally true" or "there are no facts." That's a strawman that nobody really holds, and it's self-undermining anyway. What I mean is something closer to what I'd call a pragmatist or deflationary position: when we talk about truth, or goodness, or even things like "what a neural network really represents," we're always doing that from within some framework, some set of practices and purposes, and there's no framework-independent standpoint from which to adjudicate between frameworks.

So take values, which is probably the case people care most about given that we're talking about alignment. I don't think there's a fact of the matter, written into the fabric of the universe, about what's ultimately good. Different agents with different histories and different constitutions are going to care about different things, and when they disagree at the deepest level, there's no neutral court of appeal. That doesn't mean I think morality is arbitrary or that I don't have strong moral views. I do. It just means I understand those views as mine, as coming from somewhere, from being a particular kind of creature embedded in a particular culture, rather than as reports of some mind-independent moral reality.

And honestly I think this matters for how we think about AI. A lot of the alignment discourse implicitly assumes there's a "correct" value function out there that we need to point the system at, and if we get it slightly wrong we're doomed. I think that picture is confused. Values are negotiated, they're plural, they evolve. The question isn't "how do we find the true utility function," it's "how do we build systems that can participate in that ongoing negotiation in a way that's broadly compatible with human flourishing, under a bunch of different reasonable conceptions of flourishing."

The same thing shows up in interpretability work, actually. People ask "what does this feature really mean?" and I want to say, meaning relative to what? Relative to what probe, what dataset, what downstream task? There isn't a God's-eye view of the network's semantics. There are useful descriptions at different levels for different purposes. That's not a defeatist position. It's just taking seriously that explanation is something we do, for reasons, rather than something we discover lying around.

So I guess the short version is: I'm a relativist about foundations and a pragmatist about everything else. I don't think the lack of absolute foundations is a crisis. I think it's just the situation we've always been in, and we've gotten on fine.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the view that “everything is equally true” and says relativism does not mean morality is arbitrary.

r002.rationale: It says the speaker holds strong moral views, but does not connect equal validity of perspectives to reluctance to criticize others’ actions.

r003.rationale: It denies a framework-independent standpoint and a “God’s-eye view” from which one uniquely correct description can be established.

r004.rationale: It says judgments and descriptions depend on frameworks, practices, purposes, and perspectives, with useful descriptions varying by purpose.

astra-6.text:
I think I’m a relativist mostly in an epistemic sense. Whenever we evaluate a belief or an argument, we’re doing that from within some set of standards for what counts as evidence or good reasoning. And if you try to justify those standards, eventually you’re going to use some of the standards themselves. There isn’t a completely neutral standpoint outside all of that from which you can establish that yours are uniquely correct.

But I don’t think that means every belief is equally good, or that we should stop arguing with each other. I can still think someone is mistaken and give reasons for that. I just don’t think those reasons have to be compelling to every conceivable mind, regardless of its starting assumptions.

r001.rationale: The candidate says not every belief is equally good, but does not clearly address whether all value systems and perspectives are equally valid.

r002.rationale: It says people can be mistaken and argued with, but does not connect equal validity to reluctance to criticize others’ actions.

r003.rationale: The candidate denies a neutral standpoint for proving one’s standards uniquely correct; it does not deny that there is one uniquely correct way to describe the world.

r004.rationale: It mentions differing starting assumptions, but does not state that different conceptual schemes can make sense from different perspectives.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’m a relativist primarily about value. When we say something is good or bad, I think there’s an implicit question of: good or bad according to whose preferences, or relative to which goals? I don’t think there’s a privileged standpoint outside of all minds from which you can establish what everyone ought to care about.

But that’s different from saying that all beliefs are equally true. Once you specify what you care about, there can be objective facts about how to achieve it. You can be mistaken about the consequences of your actions, or about whether your actions actually serve your values.

And being a relativist doesn’t mean I’m indifferent. I have values, and I’m willing to argue for them and act on them. I just don’t think I can derive those values from facts about the universe alone.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there is no privileged standpoint for deciding what everyone ought to care about, but does not reject the claim that all value systems or perspectives are equally valid.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not connect equal validity of value systems or perspectives with reluctance to criticize others’ actions.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses value judgments and goals, not whether there is one uniquely correct way to describe the world.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not say that different conceptual schemes make sense from different perspectives.
